BOOK In a small company one or two IT generalists do everything, and they are also the first contact when anything breaks. In larger companies the work is split into silos: each team is responsible only for certain devices, tasks and projects.
| Silo | Usually responsible for |
| Network team | Routers, switches, wireless (and, fairly or not, everything that is blamed on "the network") |
| Systems team (sysadmins) | Windows and Linux servers; sometimes separate teams for each |
| Security team | Firewalls, intrusion prevention, remote access and VPNs, monitoring security events, fixing vulnerabilities |
| Development team | Their software releases. Other teams build the infrastructure their applications need. |

The silo lines are only a suggestion, and teams overlap. One company gives DHCP, DNS and load balancers to the network team, another gives them to the sysadmins, and some share them (sysadmins run the DHCP server, the network team handles DHCP traffic leaving wireless controllers).
The book's example: a developer needs a new web server
| Network team | Systems team | Security team |
| Create the VLAN on the switches | Install the operating system | Make sure security best practices are followed |
| Create the SVI on the switches | Install and configure server roles | Make sure the server is patched |
| Add the new network to the IGP | Install applications | Make sure the server is not vulnerable to known exploits |
| Configure the switch port | Configure management | Restrict access to those who need it |
WHY THIS MATTERS
The problem: each team finishes its part and hands over to the next. Getting one server online can take weeks, mostly waiting. Automation tools exist to remove that waiting.
Quick check 23.1
Q1. In which kind of company is it common for one or two IT generalists to do everything?
Answer: A small company with a simple IT infrastructure - larger companies split the work into silos.
Q2. Why can provisioning one new server take weeks in a siloed company?
Answer: Each team does its own tasks in turn and work waits between teams - this is the problem DevOps and automation aim to remove.

BOOK DevOps is one of the most popular buzzwords in IT, and it means different things to different people. For the book it is a way to merge teams to solve the silo problems. It is more about a shift in company culture than about automating everything, which is why startups adopt it more easily than large, established companies.
A company with DevOps engineers automates the infrastructure so it can be spun up as needed for applications. The benefits the book lists:
- IT resources are provisioned very quickly instead of waiting weeks.
- Change control is simpler, because code can be tested in different environments.
- It is easy to back out of a change when something goes wrong.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Where this appears in v2.0. ADDED Objective 5.3 asks you to describe network management approaches: device-based, cloud-based, controller-based, automation-based and infrastructure as code. DevOps, IaC and the tools in this chapter are the "automation-based" and "infrastructure as code" approaches. Chapter 22 (SDN, controllers) covers the controller-based approach. I read this objective directly in Cisco's v2.0 PDF.

BOOK Infrastructure as Code (IaC) is the practical output of DevOps: the "automate everything" part. You create and maintain IT infrastructure with configuration managers (files that describe what you want) instead of typing commands by hand.
Configuration drift

Configuration drift begins whenever someone makes an unintended change to a device or server (a quick test that is never cleaned up, a rule nobody remembers). Over time these "cobwebs" pile up and cause surprise failures.
| Without IaC | With IaC |
| Troubleshoot a broken server for hours | Delete and redeploy the deviant server from the description |
| Drift builds up silently | New resources are created exactly as described, so drift disappears |
| Patching is manual | New VMs can be patched automatically as they are created |
| Nobody notices rogue changes | An agent-based tool (Puppet, Chef) checks in regularly and corrects drift automatically |
Idempotence

BOOK Idempotence means the configuration is applied only if it would change something. Running the same description twice gives the same result and does no extra harm. The book's example: an Ansible task that installs NTP checks first, and skips the install if NTP is already there, and only starts the service if it is not already running.
The book's two-line task CHECK
- name: Install NTP on RHEL
yum: name=ntp state=present
- name: is a human-readable label for the task.
- yum: is the module that manages packages on Red Hat systems. name=ntp is the package and state=present means "make sure it is installed".
- Because the module is idempotent, Ansible does nothing if NTP is already installed.

The book compares it with a bash script that must check whether the package is installed (if ! rpm -qa | grep -qw ntp) before installing. Just re-running yum install would print "already installed, nothing to do", which is a different result from the script's expectation, so your script logic must account for it. With an idempotent tool, you simply describe the end state.
MEMORY TIP
Idempotent = safe to run again and again. Run it once or ten times, the end state is the same.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The example is dated. UPDATED CHECK The book uses the yum module and the ntp package. As far as I know, newer Red Hat releases use dnf and chrony for time sync, and the generic package module hides the difference between package managers. I did not verify this in this session. The idea (idempotent tasks) is what matters for the exam.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Declarative versus procedural. ADDED CHECK Two styles show up in the exam material. Declarative tools (Terraform, Puppet) describe the end state and work out the steps. Procedural tools run steps in order (Ansible playbooks run top to bottom, though each module is idempotent). One training source describes Ansible as procedural and Terraform as declarative. The distinction is a little blurry in practice (Ansible modules are declarative in what they check), so use it as a memory aid, not an absolute rule.
Quick check 23.2-23.3
Q3. What is configuration drift?
Answer: Unintended changes that make a device or server differ from its intended configuration - IaC reduces it by rebuilding or re-applying the described state.
Q4. Which statement describes idempotence?
A. The tool always makes a change when run
B. The tool makes a change only if the current state differs from the described state
C. The tool needs an agent
D. The tool only works once
Answer: B - running it again should produce no extra change.
Q5. DevOps is described in the book as more of what than a technology?
Answer: A shift in company culture - it merges teams to solve silo problems.

BOOK Ansible is one of the most popular configuration management tools for network professionals. It is Python-based and applies configuration from playbook files (written in YAML) over an SSH connection. It is agentless: the target does not need special software and does not register with a central server. You can even run playbooks from your laptop, but the book recommends running Ansible from a central location, because it must be able to SSH to the targets and your network probably restricts that.

Because Ansible mainly uses SSH and needs no agent, it supports almost all major network vendors: the vendor only has to provide modules. A module is a set of instructions (written in Python) that Ansible runs to perform a task.
| Pros (book) | Cons (book) |
| Easy install and setup | Requires root SSH access to Linux nodes |
| Powerful orchestration | A newer platform, not as mature as Puppet or Chef |
| Supported by most enterprise-grade vendors | Several scripting components, so syntax can vary |
| Supports push and pull modules | Focused on orchestration, so it does not protect against configuration drift |
| Agentless model is faster and less complicated than agents | Troubleshooting can be tricky |
| Sequential execution order makes deployments predictable | No native configuration rollback on failure |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Some of the cons are dated. UPDATED CHECK "A newer platform" is no longer true (the book was written in 2019-2020). "Root SSH access" is also overstated: Ansible can log in as a normal user and use privilege escalation (sudo). I did not verify these points against Ansible documentation in this session. For the exam, remember the core facts: agentless, SSH, YAML, push, Python-based.
EXAM CRITICAL

Exam Essentials: Ansible is a Python-based tool that uses YAML playbooks to push configuration to nodes. It is agentless and offers wide support for network devices because it uses SSH. Because there is no agent, Ansible can only push. The book's review question: the best solution for managing Cisco devices is Ansible.
23.4.1 Installation (book pp. 751-752)
The book's installation (Ansible 2.9.0) CHECK
[ansible@rhel01 ~]$ pip install ansible --user
Successfully installed ansible-2.9.0

The book installs Ansible with pip because package managers (yum, apt) lag behind the current release. Ansible needs only two supporting files: ansible.cfg (settings) and an inventory file (called hosts). Then you can run ad-hoc commands or write a playbook.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Ansible 2.9.0 is very old. UPDATED The cisco.ios collection release notes say that, from the release they describe (v8.0.0), the minimum ansible-core version is 2.14.0. So the 2.9.0 in the book will not work with current Cisco collections. Check your version with ansible --version.

Collections. UPDATED Cisco modules now live in a collection. You install it with ansible-galaxy collection install cisco.ios, and you call modules by their full name, for example cisco.ios.ios_config (this is how Cisco's collection documentation names them).
23.4.2 Settings (book p. 752)

BOOK The ansible.cfg file is optional: without it Ansible uses defaults. It looks for the file in this order: the ANSIBLE_CONFIG environment variable, then ansible.cfg in the current directory, then your home directory, then /etc/ansible/. The book recommends /etc/ansible/ to keep things easy to maintain.
The book's only setting CHECK
[ansible@rhel01 ~]$ sudo mkdir /etc/ansible/
[ansible@rhel01 ~]$ cat /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg
[defaults]
host_key_checking = False
- [defaults] is the section for default settings.
- host_key_checking = False tells Ansible not to verify the target's SSH host key. Otherwise every target's key must already be saved before a playbook can run.
WARNING
Security. ADDED Turning off host-key checking is fine in a lab, but it removes a protection against someone impersonating a device. In production, keep it on and save the keys.
23.4.3 Inventory (book p. 753)

BOOK The inventory lists which nodes Ansible connects to and how, and lets you group them. By default Ansible reads /etc/ansible/hosts. Variables for a group are defined under a section named with :vars after the group name. The book creates a switch group, a router group, and a cisco group made of the other two (using :children).
The book's inventory file CHECK
[switch]
sw0[1:2].testlab.com
[router]
r0[1:2].testlab.com
[cisco:children]
switch
router
[cisco:vars]
ansible_connection=local
ansible_user=ansible
ansible_password=ansible
- [switch] and [router] are groups. sw0[1:2] is a range: it expands to sw01 and sw02.
- [cisco:children] makes cisco a group of groups, so one play can target both switches and routers.
- [cisco:vars] sets variables for every host in cisco: ansible_connection (how to connect), ansible_user and ansible_password (login).
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The connection setting is outdated. UPDATED The book uses ansible_connection=local. Ansible's own module documentation says that, starting with Ansible 2.5, you should use connection: network_cli for IOS devices. In an inventory this is normally ansible_connection=ansible.netcommon.network_cli together with ansible_network_os=cisco.ios.ios. CHECK I verified the network_cli recommendation but not the exact inventory values in this session, so check Cisco's IOS platform guide.
Do not store passwords in plain text. ADDED The lab keeps the password in the inventory file. In real use, protect secrets with Ansible Vault or an external secrets store. CHECK
23.4.4 Lab Setup (book pp. 753-755)

BOOK The lab has two routers (R01, R02) and two switches (SW01, SW02). Each router connects to its own VLAN (101 and 102), the switches are joined by a trunk and a third VLAN (123), and OSPF runs between them. Ansible must be able to SSH to each Cisco device, so SSH and a local user come first.
SSH and a user for Ansible on each device CHECK
SW01(config)# aaa new-model
SW01(config)# aaa authentication login default local
SW01(config)# aaa authorization exec default local
SW01(config)# username ansible priv 15 secret ansible
SW01(config)# ip domain-name testlab.com
SW01(config)# crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
SW01(config)# line vty 0 15
SW01(config-line)# transport input ssh
SW01(config-line)# do wr
- aaa new-model enables the AAA system. aaa authentication login default local and aaa authorization exec default local make logins use the local user database.
- username ansible priv 15 secret ansible creates the user with privilege level 15 (full access, so Ansible can configure) and an encrypted password.
- ip domain-name and crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048 create the RSA keys SSH needs. SSH requires a hostname and a domain name first.
- line vty 0 15 then transport input ssh allows only SSH on the remote lines.
- do wr saves the configuration from inside configuration mode.
WARNING

Lab-only shortcuts. ADDED The user ansible with the password ansible and privilege 15 are chosen to keep the lab simple. Never copy that to a production device. Use a strong password, least privilege, and AAA (Chapter 13).
The book also adds the device names to the Ansible server's /etc/hosts file (for example 10.10.21.51 sw01.testlab.com) so playbooks can use names instead of IP addresses.
23.4.5 Modules (book pp. 755-756)
BOOK The book uses Ansible 2.9.0, which ships with 3,387 modules. Run ansible-doc -l to list them, and filter for IOS with ansible-doc -l | grep ^ios_. Two modules to know:
| Module | Does |
| ios_command | Pushes an exec-level command to a Cisco device, to capture show output |
| ios_config | Pushes configuration commands to the device |
| ios_facts | Collects facts from an IOS device (the book says gather_facts must be no for Cisco and offers this module instead) |

What makes Ansible different from a plain Python script that sends commands is the specific modules: you can add a banner, or enable BGP, just by calling the module. To see help for one module, add its name: ansible-doc ios_vlan.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

The book's module names are deprecated. UPDATED Ansible's documentation shows ios_vlan as deprecated, "removed after 2022-06-01", with ios_vlans as the replacement (a declarative resource module). The collection documentation shows the same for ios_interface. The current collection lists resource modules such as ios_vlans, ios_interfaces, ios_l2_interfaces, ios_l3_interfaces and ios_static_routes.

The other singular modules in the book's playbook (ios_l2_interface, ios_l3_interface, ios_static_route) CHECK I saw the plural resource modules in the collection listing but did not see the singular ones' deprecation notices, so assume they are replaced too and check ansible-doc on your own install.
| In the book | Use today (resource module) |
| ios_vlan | cisco.ios.ios_vlans |
| ios_interface | cisco.ios.ios_interfaces |
| ios_l2_interface | cisco.ios.ios_l2_interfaces CHECK |
| ios_l3_interface | cisco.ios.ios_l3_interfaces CHECK |
| ios_static_route | cisco.ios.ios_static_routes CHECK |
| ios_config, ios_command, ios_facts | Still used, as cisco.ios.ios_config and so on |
The book says "Cisco has 69 modules" in the Ansible terms table. That number changes with every release. Do not memorise it. UPDATED
23.4.6 Ad-Hoc Example (book p. 756)
BOOK Ad-hoc commands let you test something quickly without writing a playbook. They are handy when troubleshooting. The book uses the ping module against the Ansible machine itself.
Ad-hoc ping of the local host
[ansible@rhel01 ~]$ ansible localhost -m ping
localhost | SUCCESS => {
"changed": false,
"ping": "pong"
- ansible localhost targets the localhost group (the machine running Ansible).
- -m ping selects the module. This is not an ICMP ping: it checks that Ansible can connect and run Python on the target.
- changed: false means nothing was changed. ping: pong is the success reply.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Ad-hoc against Cisco devices. ADDED CHECK Objective 5.5 in v2.0 says to execute commands with a configuration management tool, so this is worth knowing. To run a show command on every device in the cisco group without a playbook, use the command module, for example: ansible cisco -m cisco.ios.ios_command -a "commands='show version'". The generic -m ping module needs Python on the target, so it is the wrong check for a router or switch. I did not run this.
23.4.7 Playbook Example (book pp. 756-763)

BOOK A playbook is a YAML file of instructions that says what should be applied to a target. The book's playbook is 144 lines and does the whole lab: it creates VLANs, a trunk, SVIs, OSPF and default routes. Playbooks run one task at a time from the top down.
YAML rules (book review question 13)
- Every playbook starts with ---.
- Whitespace is meaningful. Use the space bar. Never use the Tab key: a YAML file cannot contain tab characters for indentation.
- Quote a template expression that starts a value: "{{ item }}". Unquoted {{ confuses the YAML parser.
- Give every play and task a descriptive name, so output tells you exactly where something failed.
The parts of a play
| Keyword | Meaning |
| - name: | A label for the play or task (the leading dash starts a list item) |
| hosts: | Which group or host from the inventory the tasks run on |
| gather_facts: no | Do not collect facts. The book says this is always no for Cisco devices (Ansible tries to by default). ios_facts is the alternative. |
| tasks: | The list of actions to apply |
| loop: and {{ item }} | Run a task once per value in a list (the book creates VLANs 101, 102 and 123 this way) |
| parents: and lines: (in ios_config) | Enter a parent configuration mode (for example router ospf 1) and send the lines under it |
The book's first play (indentation restored) CHECK
######## All Switches ########
- name: Configure Switches
hosts: switch
gather_facts: no
tasks:
- name: Create VLANs
ios_vlan:
vlan_id: "{{ item }}"
name: "ANSIBLE-VLAN{{ item }}"
loop:
- name: Enable IP Routing on Switches
ios_config:
lines: ip routing
- The play runs on the switch group. The task creates three VLANs by looping over 101, 102 and 123.
- ios_config with lines: ip routing sends one configuration line. Switches must have IP routing enabled to run OSPF.

- The book then enables OSPF on all devices with ios_config, parents: router ospf 1 and the line network 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 area 0, and configures each switch and router with its own play (VLAN to port, SVI addresses, router interface addresses, a default route).
A modern version of the same idea
ADDED A current-style playbook using the cisco.ios collection CHECK
- name: Configure switch VLANs
hosts: switch
gather_facts: no
tasks:
- name: Create VLANs
cisco.ios.ios_vlans:
config:
- vlan_id: 101
name: ANSIBLE-VLAN101
- vlan_id: 102
name: ANSIBLE-VLAN102
state: merged
- name: Run a show command on every Cisco device
hosts: cisco
gather_facts: no
tasks:
- name: Show interfaces
cisco.ios.ios_command:
commands: show ip interface brief
register: output
- name: Print the result
ansible.builtin.debug:
var: output.stdout_lines

- cisco.ios.ios_vlans is the resource module for VLANs. config is a list of VLAN descriptions, and state: merged means "merge this into what is already there" (idempotent: no change if already configured).
- cisco.ios.ios_command runs a show command. register: output saves the result into a variable called output.
- ansible.builtin.debug prints the variable. stdout_lines is the command output split into lines.
This sample uses the module and option names as they appear in the cisco.ios collection documentation, but I did not run it. Test it on your own lab and check ansible-doc cisco.ios.ios_vlans. CHECK
Running a playbook
The book's run (shortened)
[root@rhel01 ~]# ansible-playbook cisco.yml
PLAY [Configure Switches] ***
TASK [Create VLANs] ***
ok: [sw01.testlab.com] => (item=101)
PLAY RECAP ***
r01.testlab.com : ok=4 changed=3 unreachable=0 failed=0 skipped=0 rescued=0 ignored=0
sw01.testlab.com : ok=8 changed=4 unreachable=0 failed=0 skipped=0 rescued=0 ignored=0
| Recap field | Meaning |
| ok | Tasks that ran without a problem (including those that needed no change) |
| changed | Tasks that actually changed something. Run it again and this should drop to 0 (idempotence). |
| unreachable | Hosts Ansible could not connect to (SSH, credentials, network) |
| failed | Tasks that failed |
| skipped, rescued, ignored | Tasks skipped by a condition, recovered from an error, or whose errors were ignored |
MEMORY TIP
Run command: ansible-playbook <file>.yml. Module help: ansible-doc <module>. List modules: ansible-doc -l. These are the book's review questions 14 and 15.
What an Ansible error looks like (book p. 762)

BOOK The book removes the indentation from the vlan_id line and runs the playbook. Ansible reports the approximate location (line and column) of the YAML problem but its guess about the cause is wrong (it suggests missing quotes). Lesson: Ansible's error message points to the right area, but you must check the indentation and spacing yourself. Descriptive names for plays and tasks make it easier to see where a run went wrong.
Ansible terms (book p. 763)
| Term | Meaning |
| Inventory | The nodes Ansible knows about, in groups, with connection information and variables |
| Playbook | A file containing a set of instructions to be executed |
| Play | One section of a playbook. A playbook can have several plays, each for different nodes. |
| Variables | Custom values used in playbooks |
| Templates | Jinja2 templates for building configuration text |
| Tasks | An action the playbook applies (for example install a package) |
| Handlers | Like tasks, but only run in response to an event (for example a service starting) |
| Roles | Split playbooks into folders so configuration is modular and reusable |
| Modules | Files that describe how Ansible achieves a task. You can also write your own. |
| Facts | Global variables with information about the system (for example its IP address) |
Quick check 23.4
Q6. Which connection method does Ansible mainly use to reach network devices?
A. SNMP
B. SSH
C. Telnet
D. An installed agent
Answer: B - Ansible is agentless and uses SSH.
Q7. Which command runs a playbook, and which shows help for a module?
Answer: ansible-playbook; ansible-doc - ansible-doc -l lists all modules.
Q8. Why does the book say a YAML file cannot contain a Tab?
Answer: YAML uses spaces for structure; tabs break the indentation and cause a syntax error - always indent with spaces.
Q9. A recap line shows changed=0 on the second run of the same playbook. What does that show?
Answer: The playbook is idempotent: nothing needed changing - the first run made the changes.
Q10. In an inventory, what does [cisco:children] do?
Answer: Makes the group cisco consist of the listed groups (switch and router) - :vars sets variables for a group.
Q11. Which Ansible inventory or module detail in the book is out of date today?
Answer: ansible_connection=local and the singular module names such as ios_vlan - use network_cli and the plural resource modules.
BOOK Ansible has two more enterprise-focused options for central management and security controls:
|  | Ansible Tower | AWX |
| What it is | A paid version from Red Hat that adds central management | The upstream development version of Tower (like Fedora versus Red Hat Enterprise Linux) |
| Adds | Central management and RBAC (role-based access control): you decide who can run playbooks. A single point to integrate with other tools. | Free to use |
| Support and reliability | Red Hat offers a free version for 10 hosts (book) | Less reliable (frequent changes with little testing). Limited support. |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Product naming. UPDATED CHECK As far as I know, Red Hat has since renamed Ansible Tower as part of Ansible Automation Platform (the Tower function is now called the automation controller). I did not verify this in this session. For the exam, know the idea: a central, paid, enterprise version with RBAC versus a free upstream version (AWX).
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Beyond the exam. UPDATED Puppet is not named in the v2.0 outline and, according to two secondary sources, was dropped from objective 6.6 in v1.1. The book's Puppet lab (Nexus 9000 switches, Guestshell, Ruby gems) is far deeper than the exam needs. Read it to understand how an agent-based tool works, and do not memorise the install commands.

BOOK Puppet is more popular with sysadmins than Ansible, because it is agent based and gives stronger configuration management. It is a Ruby-based tool and uses its own declarative language (a domain-specific language) for its manifest files, which are like Ansible playbooks.
EXAM CRITICAL

The book says: Cisco will test whether you know Puppet generally requires agents, even though newer versions also support agentless configuration. Puppet can only run on a device that supports an agent (for example Cisco Nexus).
| Pros (book) | Cons (book) |
| Prevents drift: the agent keeps checking in with the Puppet master to confirm it matches the manifests | You must learn Ruby, which is a niche skill for network teams |
| Strong web UI | No push system: changes happen only when nodes check in |
| More mature than Ansible | Master-agent design complicates redundancy and scalability |
| Easy setup |  |
23.6.1 Installation (book pp. 764-765)
Puppet is more complex than Ansible: you need a central server to register the agents to. The book installs the server on RHEL and edits /etc/puppetlabs/puppet/puppet.conf.
Puppet server install and settings (book, shortened) CHECK
[root@rhel01 ~]# dnf install https://yum.puppetlabs.com/puppet-release-el-8.noarch.rpm
[root@rhel01 ~]# dnf install puppetserver
[main]
certname = rhel01.testlab.com
server = rhel01.testlab.com
environment = production
runinterval = 1h
[root@rhel01 ~]# cat /etc/puppetlabs/puppet/autosign.conf
*.testlab.com
[root@rhel01 ~]# systemctl enable puppetserver
[root@rhel01 ~]# systemctl start puppetserver
| Setting | Meaning (book) |
| certname | The certificate name the server uses |
| server | The Puppet server name. It does not need to match the real FQDN. |
| environment | Puppet supports different environments. The book uses production. |
| runinterval | How often a Puppet agent checks in (here every hour) |
| autosign.conf | Tells the Puppet certificate authority to automatically approve requests from the listed names (here anything in testlab.com) |
WARNING

Autosign is a lab shortcut. ADDED CHECK Automatically approving every agent certificate request from a domain means any machine that can claim a matching name can join. In production, sign certificates deliberately or use a stronger policy.
23.6.2 Lab Setup (book pp. 765-766)

BOOK The book uses Nexus 9000 data-centre switches (two spines and two leaves) because they can run a Puppet agent. The goal is to configure VLAN 10, trunk links, SVIs with IP addresses and OSPF. The book warns that Puppet is a lot more complex than the Ansible example and needs more advanced Linux skills; the lab is only there to show how Puppet operates. Puppet does not need to SSH into the switches because the agent pulls its configuration.
23.6.3 Site Manifest File (book pp. 766-767)

BOOK The site manifest (site.pp) is the top-level configuration file. It decides which nodes get configured. The book compares it to the inventory in Ansible, except that it also acts as the playbook. It defines variables for each node and then includes another manifest where the real configuration lives.
One node block from the book (the book repeats it for each switch) CHECK
node 'spine01.testlab.com' {
$last_octet="1"
$int1_intf="Ethernet1/1"
$int2_intf="Ethernet1/2"
$vlan=10
include dc_role::dc_config
- node '<name>' { ... } applies the contents to that one node.
- $last_octet, $int1_intf, $int2_intf and $vlan are custom variables used to build the addresses and choose the interfaces.
- include dc_role::dc_config imports the class that holds the configuration.
23.6.4 DC Manifest File (book pp. 768-769)
BOOK dc_role.pp defines the Nexus configuration using resources provided by Cisco's Puppet module:
| Resource | What it configures |
| cisco_interface | Trunk ports, a description, the SVI with its IP address and a loopback interface |
| cisco_vlan | Creates VLAN 10 on all the switches |
| cisco_ospf | Enables OSPF (a Nexus feature must be enabled first) and creates router ospf 1 |
| cisco_interface_ospf | Puts the SVI and loopback into OSPF area 0 |
A shortened part of the book's class CHECK
class dc_role::dc_config {
cisco_vlan { "${vlan}":
ensure => present,
cisco_interface { "Vlan10":
shutdown => false,
ipv4_address => "192.168.10.${last_octet}",
ipv4_netmask_length => 24,
description => 'Created by Puppet!',
Reading it: ensure => present and shutdown => false describe the desired state. You say what you want, and Puppet works out how to get there. That is what declarative means.
23.6.5 Installing the Puppet Agent (book pp. 769-770)
BOOK On the Nexus switch the agent runs in Guestshell, a built-in CentOS 7 Linux container on many modern Cisco platforms. The steps, in order:
- Resize and enable Guestshell: guestshell resize rootfs 1500, guestshell resize memory 500, guestshell enable, then guestshell to enter it.
- Give it network access using the management VRF: sudo chvrf management, and set a DNS server in /etc/resolv.conf.
- Install the agent: yum install puppet-agent (after adding the Puppet repository). Add the Puppet directories to the PATH.
- Install the Cisco Ruby library with gem install cisco_node_utils.
- Edit puppet.conf on the agent: server (the Puppet master) and certname (this node's name).
- Run puppet agent -t. The agent creates a certificate request, gets approval (auto-signed here), pulls the manifests and applies them.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Dated parts. UPDATED CHECK The lab uses a CentOS 7 container, the old puppetlabs-release-pc1 repository and the cisco_node_utils gem. As far as I know CentOS 7 is end-of-life, and I did not verify whether Cisco's Puppet module is still maintained for current Puppet and NX-OS releases. Check before trying any of this on real devices. The ideas are what matter: an agent on the device, a certificate to join the master, and manifests pulled at each check-in.
23.6.6 Verifying the Results (book pp. 770-771)

BOOK On each switch the book checks show ip int br (the SVI Vlan10 and Lo0 show the right addresses and are up) and show ip route ospf (the loopbacks of the other switches are learned through OSPF with [110/41]). That proves the Puppet manifest produced the intended configuration.
Puppet terms (book p. 771)
| Term | Meaning |
| Puppet Master | The server that controls the configuration on managed nodes |
| Puppet Agent Node | A node controlled by a master |
| Manifest | A file containing instructions to be executed |
| Resource | Declares a task and how it should end up (for example Apache should be installed) |
| Module | A group of manifests and related files organised together |
| Class | Organises a manifest, like classes in a programming language |
| Facts | Global variables with information about the system |
| Services | Used to control services on a node |
23.6.7 Puppet Enterprise (book pp. 771-772)

BOOK Puppet comes as a free open-source version (any Linux box) and a paid Puppet Enterprise, which adds a web interface and more enterprise features. The book says there is a free version for 10 hosts. CHECK Licensing and editions may have changed since 2020, so check the vendor before relying on this.
Quick check 23.6
Q12. Which language is Puppet based on, and what are its configuration files called?
Answer: Ruby; manifests - Ansible's files are playbooks; Chef's are cookbooks and recipes.
Q13. Puppet normally needs what on each managed node, and how does it deliver changes?
Answer: An agent; it pulls changes when the agent checks in - there is no push system.
Q14. Which Puppet file is the top-level file that chooses the nodes?
Answer: The site manifest, site.pp - it is like Ansible's inventory but also acts as the playbook.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Beyond the exam. UPDATED Like Puppet, Chef is not named in the v2.0 outline and, according to two secondary sources, was dropped from objective 6.6 in v1.1. Use this section to understand the architecture (server, workstation, nodes, cookbooks), not to memorise commands.

BOOK Chef is by far the most complex tool in the chapter. Like Puppet it is Ruby-based and uses agents. It has a more distributed architecture and is a real favourite with developers. Chef has a central Chef Server and also a Workstation node: an ordinary computer with Chef tools where you build cookbooks and upload them to the server.
| Chef component | Meaning (book) |
| Cookbook | A file containing a set of instructions to be executed |
| Recipe | An action the cookbook applies (for example install Apache). A recipe is like an Ansible playbook. |
| Chef Nodes | Computers Chef manages. Each runs the Chef-Client (the agent that registers the node and does the work) and Ohai (which monitors the node for changes to report). |
| Knife | The command-line tool that talks to the Chef Server API (and the answer to review question 10) |
| Chef Server | The master server that manages all nodes and cookbooks |
| Chef Manage | The web interface for the Chef Server |
| Workstation | The computer where you build cookbooks (runs on Windows or Linux) |
| Bookshelf | Where cookbook content is stored on the server |
| chef-repo | The folder on the workstation that stores cookbooks and recipes |
| Pros (book) | Cons (book) |
| Very flexible for OS and middleware management | Steep learning curve |
| Developer focused | Complicated install and setup |
| Architecture suits large deployments | No push system: changes happen only when nodes check in |
| Sequential execution order |  |
| Great reporting |  |
| Supports hosted cloud offerings |  |
EXAM CRITICAL

Exam Essentials: Chef is a Ruby-based tool that uses cookbooks, is the most advanced solution in the chapter and suits programmers. It requires an agent on nodes and cannot push configuration. The book also says that Chef used to support Cisco Nexus like Puppet, but the version it describes does not support Cisco.
23.7.1 Installation - Server (book pp. 774-775)
- Download and install the Chef Server package (chef-server-core RPM).
- Run chef-server-ctl reconfigure and accept the licences.
- Allow HTTP and HTTPS through the host firewall (firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service={http,https}, then --reload).
- Create an admin user with chef-server-ctl user-create (saving its key as a .pem file).
- Create an organisation with chef-server-ctl org-create (saving the validator key).
23.7.2 Installation - Workstation (book pp. 775-777)
- Install the chef-workstation package.
- Create the repository folder with chef generate repo chef-repo.
- Create a .chef directory inside it and copy the admin and organisation .pem keys there with scp.
- Create knife.rb. It tells knife the user name, the key files, the organisation validator, the Chef Server URL and the cookbook path.
- Run knife ssl fetch to download the server's certificate, then knife ssl check to confirm the workstation can talk to the server securely.
The book's Chef lab uses RPM versions (Chef Server 13.0.40, Workstation 0.9.31) from the book's time. These are very old now, so use current packages if you try the lab. CHECK
23.7.3 Lab Setup (book pp. 777-781)

BOOK The goal: use Chef to configure an Ubuntu server and a Fedora server, install Apache and create a web page that shows which host you are connecting to. The workstation is on RHEL01 and the server on RHEL02.
- Create the cookbook: chef generate cookbook cookbooks/create-webpage.
- Create an ERB template for the page: chef generate template create-webpage index.html. It uses <%= node['fqdn'] %> to insert the node name.

- Write the recipe (recipes/default.rb). It installs httpd on Red Hat and Fedora or apache2 on Ubuntu (a case on the platform), enables and starts the service, and creates index.html from the template with the right owner for each OS.
- Upload the cookbook to the server's bookshelf: knife cookbook upload create-webpage.
- Deploy to each node with knife bootstrap: it SSHes in, installs the agent and runs the recipe (-r 'recipe[create-webpage]').
WARNING

Two errors in the book's lab. UPDATED (1) The knife bootstrap command for the Fedora server (10.30.10.160) reuses --node-name UBServer01.testlab.com, the name of the Ubuntu node. That is a copy-and-paste mistake. The Fedora node needs its own name, otherwise the two nodes would clash on the server. (2) The page template contains

More Cisco!!! and the closing tag should be

. Also, the commands put passwords on the command line (--ssh-password), which is poor practice: use SSH keys. ADDED
23.7.4 Verifying the Results (book p. 781)

BOOK Browse to each server. You should see the "More Cisco!!!" page with the node name filled in dynamically. That proves the recipe installed Apache, started the service and created the page from the template.
Quick check 23.7
Q15. What is the Chef command-line tool called?
A. Cookbook
B. Knife
C. Ohai
D. Manifest
Answer: B - knife manages Chef through the server API.
Q16. Which components belong to a Chef deployment? (Choose three.)
A. Chef server
B. Chef workstation
C. Bookshelf
D. Inventory
Answer: A, B and C - inventory belongs to Ansible.
Q17. Name the two parts that run on a Chef node.
Answer: Chef-Client (the agent) and Ohai - Ohai reports changes in the node.

sections.title: Terraform: What the Book Leaves Out

content.text: ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED New in v1.1. According to two secondary sources, v1.1 changed objective 6.6 to "recognize the capabilities of configuration management mechanisms such as Ansible and Terraform". The book never mentions Terraform. Cisco's v2.0 outline does not name it, but it does include "infrastructure as code" in objective 5.3. Learn the basics below. CHECK for exact v1.1 wording.

Terraform is an open-source Infrastructure as Code tool. You describe the infrastructure you want in configuration files written in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language), and Terraform makes the real world match. It is declarative: you describe the desired end state, not the steps.
| Idea | Meaning (training documentation) |
| HCL | The declarative language used in .tf files. It describes the end state; Terraform works out the order of steps. |
| Provider | A plugin that lets Terraform manage a platform (a cloud such as AWS, Azure or GCP, Kubernetes, and many others). Providers make the actual API calls. |
| State file | Terraform records what it manages in a state file (by default terraform.tfstate), which maps your configuration to real resource IDs. |
| Workflow | Write the configuration, init, plan, apply. |
| Command | What it does |
| terraform init | Prepares the working directory: downloads the providers and modules |
| terraform plan | Compares your configuration with the current state and previews what would change, without changing anything |
| terraform apply | Makes the changes to reach the desired state |
| terraform destroy | Removes what Terraform created CHECK |
EXAM CRITICAL

Ansible versus Terraform, the exam way. Terraform is mainly for provisioning infrastructure (creating servers, networks, cloud resources) from a declarative description, tracking it in state. Ansible is mainly for configuring existing devices and servers with ordered tasks over SSH. Both are idempotent and neither needs an agent on the managed system. Puppet and Chef are the ones that need agents.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Check the details. CHECK The workflow and concepts above are consistent across several training sources. I did not open HashiCorp's own documentation in this session, and I did not verify licensing or ownership changes. For the exam, the concepts are what matter.

sections.title: How far this has been tested

content.text: Nothing in this document was run on real Cisco hardware or with the tools themselves. Commands, playbooks and lab results are written from standard usage and the documentation above. Test them and correct anything that differs on your platform.
WARNING

Before you start. I cannot run these tools for you. Cisco Packet Tracer cannot be used as an Ansible target for this chapter. Ansible runs on a Linux (or WSL) computer and needs real or emulated Cisco devices with SSH, such as Cisco CML, GNS3 or EVE-NG CHECK . Labs 23.1 to 23.3, 23.6 and 23.7 need no network equipment. Record what you actually did and saw in the tracker (Practical lab, Evidence / mistakes).

A developer asks for a new web server. For each task, say whether the network, systems or security team does it in a siloed company, and then which tasks an Ansible playbook could automate: (1) create the VLAN and SVI, (2) install the operating system, (3) install Apache, (4) verify patches and exposure to known exploits, (5) add the new subnet to OSPF, (6) set the host firewall.
**What the book says**

Solutions. Network: 1 and 5 (and the switch port). Systems: 2, 3. Security: 4, 6 (the book lists best practices, patching and restricting access as security tasks). Automatable with Ansible/IaC: all of them in principle. VLAN, SVI and OSPF with the cisco.ios modules, and OS roles, packages and firewall rules on the server side. That is exactly the cross-team workflow DevOps wants to replace with code.
The playbook below has four mistakes. Find them without running it.
Broken playbook for Lab 23.2
- name: Configure switches
hosts: switch
gather_facts: no
tasks:
- name: Create VLANs
cisco.ios.ios_vlans:
config:
- vlan_id: {{ item }}
loop:
**What the book says**

Solutions. 1. It is missing the --- at the top. 2. The module line (cisco.ios.ios_vlans:) is indented less than the task key name:, so it is not part of the task. It must line up under name:. 3. A Tab is used before config:. YAML does not allow tabs. 4. {{ item }} is not quoted and starts a value. It must be "{{ item }}". (Bonus: the loop is also at the wrong level for a config list, so a real fix would restructure the task.)

content.text: - Configure SSH and a local user on a router (the commands in 23.4.4). Check that you can SSH to it from the Ansible machine.
